text: Three generations of one family share the same few rooms, and the camera is close enough to be another body in the house. Leonard Retel Helmrich made the film in Indonesia and in Indonesian, on Dutch money, and its ninety-two minutes stay with that household rather than with the country behind it: the largest Muslim population on earth registers here as a kitchen, a roof, a doorway someone is standing in. Money, faith, and the ordinary friction between a grandmother, her son, and the child growing up between them carry what a thesis would carry elsewhere. Sundance's world documentary jury gave it their grand prize, which for a film this domestic is worth pausing on. Proximity is the method: who defers to whom, and how often, becomes legible without anyone stopping to explain it.

The people at the centre of this film write, teach and argue in public against religious and nationalist fundamentalism, and in India that has become dangerous work. Anand Patwardhan follows them for two hundred and eighteen minutes, and the length is not a flourish: his case is cumulative, and a cumulative case falls apart the moment it is compressed to the shape of a news segment. In Hindi, at ground level, with the connective tissue left in. Secular rationalism sounds like an abstraction until it is attached to particular people who can be named, followed, and hunted. Three and a half hours across a country that size is still a sample, and Patwardhan knows it. He does not hurry toward a verdict; he lets the record pile up until its shape stops being arguable.

The fighting is over for these men, and it is the part that comes afterward that Laurent Bécue-Renard set out to film. Five years at a clinic in California, where veterans work on what combat left inside them, cut to a hundred and forty-two minutes; the length is the only honest measure of how slowly this kind of repair moves. A French production of an American subject, which gives the film an outsider's patience with silence. Men talk, and what they are trying to say does not come out on schedule. The European Film Award for best documentary went to a picture with almost no incident in it, which is a fair indication of what Bécue-Renard is after: not the story of a war, but the labour of coming back from one, done slowly and out loud.

Soghomon Vardanyan was twenty-one, a student and a musician, and near the end of his mandatory military service when the fighting over Artsakh flared again in September 2020. The number in this film's title is the one assigned to the body of an individual missing in action; it was assigned to him. Shoghakat Vardanyan, who made the film, shares his surname. Seventy-six minutes, in Armenian, at the scale of a household rather than a front: what a war does to the people who are not in it, which is mostly waiting, and the daily business that does not stop for waiting. Reports print numbers because numbers fit in a column. This is what one of those numbers looks like from inside the house it came from.

The Pont-Neuf is stone, and old, and the proposal is to cover the whole of it in cloth. Albert Maysles gives that idea fifty-eight minutes. Christo and Jeanne-Claude are the two people asking; Paris is a city with settled opinions about its own bridges; so the film's work becomes the project's work, which is drawings, arguments, permissions, and the long stretch in which the thing exists only as a claim that has to keep being defended out loud. A wrapping is a proposal before it is an object, and a proposal is made of meetings. What makes the pair worth an hour is not the gesture but the stamina behind it, two artists treating municipal process as a material, the way someone else treats fabric or stone.

Two people who grew up together in Cuba now live in another country, and the camera is how they keep talking. In a Whisper puts the making of the film inside the friendship, so that the record of leaving and the act of staying in touch become the same act. Patricia Pérez Fernández works in Spanish, in eighty minutes, at the scale of what a life actually holds: motherhood, the love of cinema, the practical business of being uprooted while a friend from childhood is uprooted somewhere else. Autoethnography is a heavy word for a film this quiet. The structural move is the interesting one, two filmmakers who are each both author and subject. What accumulates is less an account of exile than an account of maintenance: what two people spend on not becoming strangers.

In 1988, on a street eight hundred metres long at the edge of Riga, Ivars Seleckis went from house to house. That is the whole territory of the film: who lives where, what a day consists of, how the neighbours are managed. The Awakening was underway in Latvia while the camera ran, and nobody in front of it is asked to summarize what that means; the period arrives instead through what people do about their own street. Ninety-three minutes, in Latvian, produced under the Soviet state the street still belonged to, and given the European Film Award for best documentary the year after. Seleckis is interested in the person a newsreel would file as average, and not sentimentally. He is making a claim about where a country can be read: between neighbours, one house at a time.

A box of colour slides turned up in a Vienna second-hand bookshop in 1987. The man who took them had been chief accountant of the Lodz ghetto. Walter Genewein's assignment was output against cost, and he was efficient enough that the ghetto he administered outlasted every other in Poland; the photographs are the work of a bookkeeper who cared about exposure and colour fidelity, pointed at people he had decided were less than human. Dariusz Jabłoński takes fifty-two minutes and refuses the terms the images arrived with, turning them toward the experience of the people trapped inside them. The difficulty is not atrocity footage. It is competence, and it is colour, which makes the ghetto look like somewhere a person could walk into: precisely what Genewein was not seeing.

Six years old and seventy-five years old, in the same house, and neither of them inclined to give ground. Adán Aliaga's film is filed as comedy and drama as well as documentary, which is honest: the material is a child and a grandmother disagreeing about how a person ought to live, and that kind of disagreement is funny for exactly as long as it is not. Eighty minutes, in Spanish, at domestic scale and no larger. The grandmother's convictions were formed in a Spain that moved on without consulting her; the child's come from wherever children get them, and are equally non-negotiable. Rebellion at that age, in a house that size, is built out of small refusals. The comedy lives in the mismatch. The drama is that neither of them has anywhere else to be.

Three thousand miles upriver, undertaken by a man whose legs have not carried him since childhood. Jamana Lal is thirty-five and devout; his mother has died, the journey to Haridwar is made in her name, and his brother and his wife travel with him, along with Pirjo Honkasalo and her small crew. She shot it on 35mm, which for a documentary covering that distance is a decision with consequences: the stock is finite and heavy, every setup costs something, and the seventy-six minutes look composed rather than harvested. It closes the trilogy Honkasalo called The Trilogy of the Sacred and the Satanic, though what the camera mostly attends to is logistics. How a body that cannot walk covers ground. Who lifts it, and where the Ganges serves as a road and where it does not.

What the two boys intend to do with their first professional wages is throw a barbecue. Leonardo and Anselmo are eleven, they live in a favela in Rio, and it is the summer of 1994, the World Cup playing in the United States with Brazil favoured to win it. Which makes their arithmetic, football or nothing much, the most ordinary arithmetic in the country that season. Jos de Putter takes fifty-four minutes and keeps the scale honest: the boys play for Nova Saffra, a side run out of a home for poor children, the whole institutional backing the ambition has. Other kids on the same streets talk about becoming fishermen. What holds the film together is how precise the dream is. Not fame, not money as an abstraction, but meat on a grill for people they already know.

At the edge of a Romanian landfill there is a settlement, and the film goes no further than that. Andrej Schwartz spends seventy-five minutes on a single arrangement between a place and the people living at its rim, Roma families whose address is the tip. A documentary built this way trades range for duration: one location, one economy, nothing to cut away to when the material turns uncomfortable. The camera is German and the ground is Romanian, and the gap between them is a condition of the work rather than a flaw in it. What a visiting crew can record honestly is rhythm: when the day starts, what the ground yields, how an unplanned settlement organizes itself anyway. Proximity to waste is not a figure of speech here. It is an address and a set of hours.
